Pac-Man

There's a reason it was a sensation in the early 80, in a world where video games existed and were kind of "neat" but didn't really embrace the public like the little yellow pizza did:

  1. The goal to go the next stage is eat all the pellets, an action that's completely passive.

  2. That goal also makes it easy to figure out where you have to go to wrap things up.

  3. Also encourages "collect everything" behavior, which helps a lot in games even to this day. Examples: pick up ammo refills before boss, health as you see them, coins for free lives...

  4. And they're scattered in a maze. Everyone knows what mazes are. The maze is simple and has no dead ends, so the player is free to go around but still gets constrained by the game.

  5. Oh, and, the controls are dead simple. Even if a first-time gamer doesn't know about holding a direction versus tapping, the game is forgiving.

  6. Speaking of first time gaming, a player learns everything after the intro music. Ghosts are in a box, the yellow thing appears. "That must be me!"

  7. Ghosts put pressure but each does it's own thing. Eventually a player can figure out that Red gets faster the more pellets get eaten, Blue likes to take the long way around. These little realizations are subtle, and even if they don't consciously "get it", their brain does. They can understand the concept of enemies.

  8. Power pellets change game state, and it's obvious the tables turn: ghosts change direction and slow down, sound changes. It begs the player to find out what happens now when you get in their way. The player is living in the world.

  9. Changes back to normal state in a very conspicuous way. Teaches to make the most of things while you've got them. Compounding bonus scores also reinforce this. Learn timing things just right.

  10. Easy failure modes, collide with a ghost. Yellow dude disintegrates, negative reinforcement, do better.

  11. Fruit is a thrill, take a chance and get more points but get lead right back into the middle of the maze. Decision making beyond the maze. You can choose to make things harder on yourself for a bonus.

  12. SCORE. It's easy to quantify progress in the game: 100K points, 200K points, etc.

All this combines, in my opinion, to make this the end-all tutorial video game for the entire video game world. So many of these elements are refined and expanded for modern games. Levels are essentially upgraded mazes, sometimes more complicated, sometimes less, definitely prettier. Enemies have vulnerabilities that involve timing and being in the right place at the right time doing the right thing. You can explore and find hidden fruits even if it's out of your way. You connect with a central figure and it's obvious who it is even if you miss an intro cutscene.
